title: A Prophet at Breaking Point
overview: God declares that judgment on Jerusalem can no longer be turned back, and Jeremiah, worn out by rejection, pours out his anger and pain to God and is answered.

parts.label: Beyond pleading (vv. 1-4)
parts.note: Moses and Samuel were remembered for praying Israel out of trouble, so saying even they could not help means the coming disaster is fixed. It is linked to Manasseh, an earlier king remembered for idol worship and killing innocent people, whose ways the nation kept following.

parts.label: Jerusalem left alone (vv. 5-9)
parts.note: Winnowing was tossing grain so the wind carried off the husks; here it pictures the people scattered from their land. The images are brutal and meant to be: widows beyond counting, a destroyer striking at midday, and a once blessed mother of seven whose sun sets while it is still day.

parts.label: Jeremiah's lament (vv. 10-11)
parts.note: Jeremiah wishes he had never been born, since everyone curses him though he has given no cause, which is what never lending or borrowing means. God promises him good, and the book later tells of enemies treating him well and leaders seeking his help, though the Hebrew of verse 11 is hard to translate.

parts.label: Iron from the north (vv. 12-14)
parts.note: This most likely means Judah cannot break the hard power coming from the north, Babylon, though scholars debate the exact sense. The nation's wealth will be handed over as worthless loot and its people taken to a foreign land.

parts.label: Joy turned to accusation (vv. 15-18)
parts.note: Jeremiah asks God to remember him and pay back his persecutors, recalling how he once took in God's words with delight and lived alone because of his message. Then he accuses God of being like a stream that runs dry in summer, failing just when it is needed most.

parts.label: God's answer (vv. 19-21)
parts.note: God calls Jeremiah himself to turn back and speak what is worthy rather than worthless, letting the people come to him instead of bending to them. The promise to make him a bronze wall repeats the promise made when Jeremiah was first called.

disagreement: Christians differ on whether Jeremiah's bitter complaint in verse 18 was a failing God corrected with a call to repent, or an honest lament God welcomed and answered with renewed promises.
think: When standing by what you believe leaves you isolated and resented, what makes it worth continuing, if anything?
